newsitem.title: USA: Budget deal has tax cuts for investors, families.
newsitem.headline: Budget deal has tax cuts for investors, families.

text.p: Americans would see a net tax cut of $85 billion over five years if a budget deal between the White House and congressional leaders announced on Friday is enacted.
The agreement sketched broad outlines of what would be included in a package of $135 billion gross tax cuts over five years, offset by about $50 billion in tax increases.

A capital gains tax cut pushed by Republicans since the start of the year would be included, giving investors who make money by selling assets such as stocks a lower tax rate. The top capital gains tax rate is currently 28 percent.
Republicans promised President Clinton that his desired tax relief for college tuition would be included, expected to cost about $35 billion over five years.

The package would include a $500 child credit which appears to have general support and estate tax relief on inheritances, something sought by Republicans. The estate tax kicks in on an inheritance above $600,000, and Republicans have pushed to raise that threshold.
Provisions to expand eligibility for Individual Retirement Accounts would also be part of a tax package.
Clinton acknowledged that Democrats believed the tax cuts were too steep while Republicans believed spending for programmes like education was too high.

"The Democrats will think the tax cuts are too big and too skewed to people with high incomes, and Republicans will think we're investing too much in education and other things," Clinton said. "And I'm sure there will be some on both sides who won't vote for it," he added.

While the budget accord was a general agreement, the specifics of the tax cuts, such as a new capital gains tax rate, will be written in the House Ways and Means Committee, where all tax legislation originates.

One of the last sticking points to a budget deal was that the chairmen of the House and Senate tax-writing committees insisted they wanted control over filling in the specifics within the parameters of a tax cut number.
The White House put up a fight on that issue, wanting more tax specifics included in the budget agreement before signing off on it.
Initial responses to the budget accord showed some Republicans and Democrats were unhappy with the outlined tax package.

"I do not know all of the details of the agreement, but I must say that I am disappointed by the small size of the tax cut," said Senate Finance Committee Chairman William Roth. The Delaware Republican, head of the Senate tax-writing committee, had been pushing for about $140 billion in net tax cuts.
The ranking Democrat on the House Ways and Means Committee expressed the feelings shared by many in his party that the tax cuts will help the wealthy at the expense of programmes for the poor.

"I have not decided whether to endorse this budget package," Representative Charles Rangel, a New York Democrat, said. He said his two concerns were "the important details are yet to be determined and the people who benefit from the tax cuts are not my constituents."
"It certainly has a variety of different themes to it," said Peter Merrill, national director for tax policy economics at Price Waterhouse LLP.

The capital gains tax cut was intended to encourage investment and savings, the child credit would be relief for middle class families, and the estate tax would help the "very richest individuals," he said. "This is a real potpourri that has different political and economic reasons," Merrill said.
